analysis.one_liner: Cancels Medicare Advantage contracts whose coverage denials get overturned too often on appeal.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 2025 and referred to two House committees; no vote has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare Advantage plans are private insurance plans paid by Medicare. Under this bill, if Medicare finds that a plan wrongly denies requests for prior approval of care more than 25% of the time — meaning the denial gets reversed when the patient appeals — the government would have to cancel that plan's Medicare contract. It also blocks a plan from avoiding the rule simply by approving fewer appeals.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans, especially those whose requests for scans, surgeries, therapy, or medications get denied and only approved after an appeal. If a plan denies care wrongly more than 25% of the time, its contract ends, so patients would either get faster approvals or a route out of a bad plan.

how_it_helps.text: If more than 25% of a plan's prior authorization denials are later reversed on reconsideration or appeal in a year, Medicare must terminate that plan's contract, so enrollees would no longer be stuck in a plan that wrongly denies care at scale.

The bill also lets the Secretary terminate a plan if reversed denials suddenly drop because the plan stopped properly reconsidering denials — closing a loophole where a plan could lower its reversal rate by suppressing appeals rather than approving deserved care.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers, which would face contract termination — losing all their plan's enrollees and revenue — if too many of their coverage denials are reversed on appeal.

drawbacks.text: The trigger is a hard contract termination, the harshest enforcement tool available; plans near the line might respond by dropping Medicare Advantage offerings or restricting service areas rather than improving their decisions, potentially reducing plan choices for seniors.

A fixed 25% threshold is a blunt measure: some reversals reflect legitimate patient appeals rather than bad-faith denials, and plans might game the number by discouraging appeals or slowing reconsiderations instead of approving deserved care.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: wrongly denied care would be restored and insurers would face a strong reason to stop over-denying, reducing delays and financial strain for older adults. The main drawback is design risk — a hard 25% contract-termination trigger could discourage MA plans from using prior authorization at all or push them to drop plans, and the 25% threshold is somewhat arbitrary; more calibrated penalties might be a safer tool. On balance the mechanism targets a documented harm but carries enforcement-heavy tradeoffs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the House and sent to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 18, 2025 and referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees; no further action has been taken.
It has 18 cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 435 House members.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers are better off so far, since the bill remains stalled in committee and their prior authorization denials remain unconstrained by it.

for.name: Rep. Mark Pocan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create denial-reversal rate requirements for Medicare Advantage plans.

for.name: 18 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Jayapal, Ocasio-Cortez, Khanna, DeLauro, Tlaib, and Schakowsky.

against.name: House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; no Republicans have signed on.

industries.note: Plans that deny care too aggressively would risk losing their Medicare contract under the reversal-rate trigger. The bill constrains their ability to use prior authorization denials to hold down medical payouts.

analysis.trajectory: With a referral to two committees, no Republican cosponsors, and no scheduled committee action, the bill is likely to sit until the Congress ends, as first-term prior-authorization bills routinely do without leadership backing.
